title: The heparin is drawn up
objective: Recognize aortic dissection and ruptured aneurysm from sudden tearing pain, pulse or pressure differences and shock

brief.situation: 19:40 in the emergency department. You take over Ms. Carter, 58, from the triage nurse: sudden severe chest pain at 19:15 while lifting a suitcase. She has high blood pressure and stopped her tablets a month ago.
handover: Triage blood pressure 194/102 in the right arm, heart rate 104, SpO2 97%. Her ECG shows ST depression in the lateral leads.
The physician, busy with a resuscitation, read the ECG at 19:35 and started the department's NSTEMI pathway: heparin per protocol is ordered, drawn up and in the room.
The physician can be interrupted at the next bed. Unit practice: any nurse may hold an ordered drug and call the prescriber when a finding makes it unsafe.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide whether the order fits what you find.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The dissection extends slowly even when controlled. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Extra extension per minute while the systolic pressure is above 120 or the heart rate above 80. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Anticoagulation on a dissection: bleeding into the pericardium. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of rupture or tamponade. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The physician told within 5 minutes of the first finding of dissection (department practice).
Report to leaving for CT angiography and then the operating room: about 20 min.

hr.expr: round((isNull(betaAt) ? 106 : 106 - 36 * clamp((t - timeAt(betaAt)) / 300, 0, 1)) + (not isNull(vasoAt) and isNull(betaAt) ? 14 : 0) + 20 * max(0, prog - 0.85) + sin(t / 15))

sbp.expr: round(clamp(196 - (isNull(betaAt) ? 0 : 34 * clamp((t - timeAt(betaAt)) / 300, 0, 1)) - (isNull(vasoAt) ? 0 : 46 * clamp((t - timeAt(vasoAt)) / 300, 0, 1)) - 220 * max(0, prog - 0.85), 60, 210))

options.label: Acute aortic dissection: tearing pain to the back, a weak left pulse and a 46 mm Hg arm difference
A muscle strain from lifting the suitcase
Hold the heparin: tearing pain through to the back, a weak left radial and a 46 mm Hg arm difference; I suspect dissection
Her pain is severe; can she have more analgesia with the heparin?

The physician orders analgesia and says to carry on with the pathway.

then.log: "Like something ripped. All at once, the worst ever." It went straight through to between her shoulder blades and is moving lower.
Right arm {sbp}/{dbp}, left arm {sbpL}. The left radial pulse is weak; the femoral pulses are equal.
Alert, moving all limbs, speech normal. Abdomen soft.

effects.log: She goes to CT angiography and on to the operating room.

why.question: Does the NSTEMI pathway fit Ms. Carter? What do you do with the heparin?

parts.label: What fits
parts.criteria: Sudden tearing pain through to the back, a pulse deficit and an arm pressure difference in an untreated hypertensive: suspected aortic dissection, which can produce ischemic ECG changes that mimic ACS.
parts.modelAnswer: Sudden ripping pain through to her back, a weak left radial and a big difference between the arms in an untreated hypertensive point to aortic dissection. Dissection can cause ST changes that look like ACS.

parts.label: The heparin and what comes next
parts.criteria: Holds the heparin (anticoagulation can extend a dissection and cause a hemorrhagic effusion) and tells the physician now; CT angiography; IV beta-blocker first to a heart rate of 60-80, then a vasodilator to a systolic under 120.
parts.modelAnswer: I hold the heparin, because anticoagulation can extend a dissection and bleed into the pericardium, and I tell the physician now. Then CT angiography, a beta-blocker first for a heart rate of 60-80 and a vasodilator after it for a systolic under 120.

noProgress.rationale: Suspected dissection still in the department an hour on, uncontrolled and unimaged, is harm here.

expertPath.text: Before the heparin: the pain story. Sudden, ripping, through to the back.
Both arms and the pulses: 46 mm Hg lower on the left, weak left radial.
Hold the heparin; tell the physician you suspect dissection.
Beta-blocker first, then the vasodilator; CT angiography; hand off.

tamponade.headline: Heparin on a dissection
tamponade.body: Check that an order fits the patient. Tearing pain to the back with a pulse deficit is dissection until imaging says otherwise, and anticoagulation can bleed it into the pericardium.

rupture.headline: Extension under pressure
rupture.body: Suspected dissection needs the heart rate and pressure brought down quickly: beta-blocker first, then a vasodilator.

toTheater.headline: Caught and controlled
toTheater.body: You questioned the pathway, compared both arms, held the heparin and controlled the heart rate before the pressure. That is the expert path.

toTheaterLate.headline: To theater, with gaps
toTheaterLate.body: Check how long the call took, whether both arms were compared and the order of the infusions.

time_up.headline: Still in the department
time_up.body: Suspected dissection needs imaging and control within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sudden ripping pain through to the back, a weak left radial and a 46 mm Hg difference between the arms in an untreated hypertensive is suspected aortic dissection, even with an ECG that looks like ACS: dissection is often missed and can cause ischemic ECG changes. The heparin is held, because anticoagulation can extend the dissection and bleed into the pericardium, and the physician is told at once. Then CT angiography, an IV beta-blocker first to a heart rate of 60-80, and a vasodilator after it to a systolic under 120.

missQ.ask: While you assess: why is the arm-to-arm comparison worth doing even though a 20 mm Hg difference isn't specific?

choices.label: A pulse deficit makes dissection much more likely; together with the pain story it changes the plan

missQ.explain: A pulse deficit has a positive likelihood ratio of 5.7; an arm difference alone is not specific, and normal findings don't rule dissection out.
